growth_story.headline: Uzbekistan grew fastest in the 2006–2015 commodity boom; since 2016 income per person has grown more slowly but steadily, reaching a new high in 2025.
growth_story.arc: After independence, income per person fell by 3.6 percent a year over 1990–1997, though output fell less than in other former Soviet economies, helped by rising world prices for cotton. Under a gradual reform that kept a high level of state control, income per person grew 3.5 percent a year over 1998–2005 and did not pass its 1990 level until 2006. Growth then rose to 6.4 percent a year over 2006–2015, carried by high world prices for the country's export commodities. Falling commodity prices from mid-2014 and Russia's 2014–2015 crisis slowed growth, and after President Karimov's death in 2016 the government began in 2017 to free the currency and prices and open the economy. Over 2016–2025 income per person grew 4.1 percent a year, slower than in the boom decade but steady, while investment rose sharply, and it reached a new high in 2025.

threads.title: A gradual exit from planning
threads.text: After independence the government moved slowly away from central planning, freeing some prices, especially for energy and fuel, while keeping a high level of state control. Output fell less than in other former Soviet economies, helped by rising world prices for cotton, then the main export.

threads.title: Commodity boom, then a bust
threads.text: From 2004 to 2015 growth was fast and rested on high world prices for the country's exports. From mid-2014, lower prices for gas, gold and copper and a financial crisis in Russia cut exports and the money migrant workers sent home.

threads.title: The 2017 opening
threads.text: Before 2017, policy favoured state intervention, import substitution and controls on foreign exchange. In September 2017 the government freed the currency market, and reforms to prices and state firms followed. The IMF and the World Bank both link growth since then to this turn to the market.

threads.title: Investment, credit and the state
threads.text: Investment rose from 20.2 percent of GDP in 2016 to 35.3 percent in 2019 and was 34.0 percent in 2025, while bank credit to the private sector grew from 10.3 to 31.2 percent of GDP between 2016 and 2025. The IMF lists directed and preferential lending among the risks, and the World Bank says state dominance and directed lending leave many smaller firms short of credit.

threads.title: Gold and money from abroad
threads.text: High gold prices helped narrow the budget deficit in 2025, and money sent home by workers abroad, mostly from Russia, remains large. Remittances eased a little in the first half of 2026, while gold exports fell back after strong growth a year earlier.

since_last_year.text: Growth picked up. Income per person grew 5.7 percent in 2025, the fastest since 2021, and the economy kept speeding up into 2026 on strong spending by households and on investment. In June 2026 the IMF judged that the economy is probably running above its potential.

growth_story.tension: The IMF and the World Bank describe the years since 2017 as a reform success and recent growth as strong. The data agree that income per person is at a new high, but they show the decade since 2016 growing more slowly, at 4.1 percent a year, than the commodity-boom decade before it, at 6.4. Part of the gap between the fast GDP growth the sources report and the slower rise in income per person reflects a growing population.
